reports.text:
Indication: microscopic hematuria.
Right kidney 10.9 cm, left kidney 11.2 cm. Normal cortical echogenicity and thickness. No hydronephrosis, stone or solid mass on either side. Bladder adequately distended with smooth wall and no intraluminal lesion. Prostate appears enlarged, indenting the bladder base.
reports.conclusion: Normal kidneys. Enlarged prostate. No renal or bladder mass seen.

documents.title: Urology consultation and cystoscopy
documents.author: urology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE UROLOGY GROUP — Consultation and procedure note, 04/20/2018
Reason: persistent microscopic hematuria. 67M, former smoker (25 pk-yr, quit 2010), BPH on tamsulosin. Renal ultrasound from PCP reviewed: normal kidneys, enlarged prostate. CT urography avoided because of contrast anaphylaxis.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Procedure: Flexible diagnostic cystoscopy under local anesthetic. Urethra normal. Prostate with enlarged, coapting lateral lobes. Bladder mucosa normal throughout with no tumor, stone, or diverticulum. Ureteral orifices normal in position with clear efflux.
Impression: Microscopic hematuria, no bladder pathology. Likely related to prostatic enlargement.
Plan: Continue tamsulosin. Repeat UA with routine care; return for any visible blood.
Urologist

OUTSIDE PAIN MANAGEMENT CLINIC — Follow-up note, 11/23/2018
Subjective: Scheduled visit for chronic lumbar stenosis pain. He feels the morphine ER 60 mg twice a day is no longer holding him; pain most days 6-7/10. No falls or injury. No new weakness, numbness, or bladder or bowel change.
Meds: morphine ER 60 mg q12h, morphine IR 15 mg q4h prn, metformin, lisinopril, HCTZ, tamsulosin, atorvastatin, aspirin 81.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives); iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Vitals: BP 142/88, HR 78, RR 16.
Exam: Tender over the lower lumbar spine and paraspinals, skin without redness or warmth. Strength, sensation and reflexes in the legs normal; gait normal.
Data: PCP labs 11/08: A1c 7.2%, eGFR 58.
Assessment: Lumbar spinal stenosis, pain suboptimally controlled on morphine; reduced kidney function.
Plan: We talked through rotating from morphine to a different long-acting opioid that is handled better with reduced kidney function, with a calculated conversion. He prefers to stay on his current medicine for now rather than switch. Morphine regimen continued unchanged; activity pacing and home exercise reviewed. Return 3 months.
Pain management physician

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Neck pain and gait
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: About 3 months of worsening neck pain. When he bends his head down he gets an electric jolt down his back. Walking feels harder, 'like my legs don't listen.' Different from his usual lumbar pain. No falls, no bladder change, no trauma.
O: Vitals as charted. Neck flexion reproduces the shock sensation. Grip seems weaker than I recall; knee reflexes brisk. Gait slightly wide. Exam otherwise as before.
A/P: Neck pain with shock sensations on flexion and gait change in a man with known cervical spondylosis: concern for cervical cord compression. Neurology referral, urgent slot requested; they will order MRI (no contrast needed; gadolinium not the same as his iodine allergy, but they can decide). Return precautions for weakness, falls or bladder change.

documents.title: Neurology consultation, 06/04/2019
documents.author: neurology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE NEUROLOGY — Consultation letter, visit 06/04/2019

Dear colleague,
Thank you for referring Mr. Mayhew, 68, with half a year of increasing neck pain, a harder time walking, and shock-like sensations running down his back whenever he flexes his neck. This began roughly six months after his last pain-clinic review of his lumbar stenosis. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes.
Medications: metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg, HCTZ 12.5 mg, tamsulosin 0.4 mg qhs, morphine ER 60 mg BID, morphine IR 15 mg q4h prn, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 81 mg.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).

Examination: Wasting of the intrinsic hand muscles bilaterally with reduced grip. Biceps and triceps jerks reduced. Knee jerks 3+, with sustained clonus at both ankles. Right plantar response extensor; left flexor.

Recent labs from your office: A1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 156, total cholesterol 210, HDL 40, LDL 130, triglycerides 200.

MRI cervical spine without contrast (06/04/2019): multilevel degenerative disease with disc-osteophyte complexes narrowing the spinal canal at several levels.

Impression: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy, multilevel.
Plan: Referral to spine surgery to discuss decompression. Fall precautions. Neurology follow-up after the surgical opinion.

Neurologist

documents.title: Spine surgery consultation, 07/22/2019
documents.author: spine surgery
documents.body:
OUTSIDE SPINE SURGERY — Consultation, 07/22/2019
Referred by neurology for cervical spondylotic myelopathy. 69M with neck pain, gait difficulty and flexion-induced shocks; MRI with multilevel degenerative canal narrowing. Exam today consistent with the neurology findings: hand intrinsic wasting, hyperreflexia in the legs with ankle clonus.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics, iodinated contrast.
Discussion: We reviewed multilevel posterior decompression versus nonoperative management with close surveillance, including risks of surgery at his age with diabetes and chronic opioid use, and the risk of progression without surgery. After discussion with his wife he prefers nonoperative care for now.
Plan: Nonoperative management. Physical therapy for balance and gait. Avoid neck manipulation. Neurology to follow; return to us for any decline in hand function, walking or bladder control.
Spine surgeon

documents.title: Blurred vision, headaches, dizziness
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Two months of blurry vision in both eyes (not just the cataract eye), dull headaches most days, spells of dizziness lasting minutes, and pins and needles in the hands and feet. Not the same as his neck shocks. No new weakness, no speech trouble, no falls. No fevers, no night sweats.
O: Vitals as charted. Conjunctivae pale. Undilated fundi hard to see. Neuro: reduced light touch in the feet and hands in a stocking-glove pattern; strength unchanged from his baseline; speech normal. Heart regular, lungs clear.
A/P: New symptom cluster with pallor. Not typical for TIA (no focal deficit, constant over weeks). Check CBC, CMP; add protein electrophoresis if total protein is high. Low threshold for ED if focal symptoms. Will call with results.

documents.title: Initial labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hgb 10.2, MCV 89 (new normocytic anemia). Creatinine 1.4, calcium 9.2. Total protein 9.8 with albumin 3.2: big globulin gap. Added SPEP/immunofixation to today's sample.

orders.reason: monoclonal protein 3.4 g/dL, anemia, possible hyperviscosity symptoms

documents.title: Results call: monoclonal protein
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called pt and wife. SPEP shows a monoclonal spike, 3.4 g/dL in the gamma region; immunofixation typing to follow. Together with the anemia, high protein and his vision and headache symptoms, I am worried about a blood protein disorder that can thicken the blood. Spoke directly with hematology-oncology on call; they will see him 6/5, sooner if symptoms worsen. Told them to go to the ED for confusion, worsening vision, bleeding, or severe headache. Wife mentioned his uncle had 'a blood protein cancer.' They understand.

reports.text:
Specimen: Bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy, right posterior iliac crest.
Microscopic: Hypercellular marrow with an interstitial and nodular infiltrate of small lymphocytes, many with plasmacytoid features, admixed with plasma cells. Trilineage hematopoiesis present but reduced. Flow cytometry: monotypic B-cell population with lambda light chain restriction. Molecular: MYD88 L265P mutation detected.
reports.conclusion: Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma involving bone marrow, consistent with Waldenström macroglobulinemia in the setting of an IgM lambda paraprotein.

documents.title: Hematology-oncology consultation, 06/05/2020
documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CANCER CENTER, HEMATOLOGY-ONCOLOGY — New patient consultation, 06/05/2020

Referred for monoclonal protein and anemia. 69M with cervical myelopathy and lumbar stenosis (followed by neurology and pain management), HTN and T2DM on metformin and lisinopril. Two months of blurred vision, headaches, dizzy spells, and tingling in hands and feet.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (hives), iodinated contrast (anaphylaxis).
Family history: maternal uncle with Waldenström macroglobulinemia.

Exam: Pale conjunctivae. Fundoscopy shows engorged retinal veins bilaterally. Diminished light-touch sensation in a stocking-glove distribution.

Data: PCP labs 05/19: Hgb 10.2, MCV 89, creatinine 1.4, calcium 9.2, total protein 9.8, albumin 3.2, M-spike 3.4 g/dL (gamma). Today: IgM 4,850 mg/dL; immunofixation IgM lambda; serum viscosity elevated at 4.8 cP. Bone marrow biopsy performed today (report attached).

Assessment: Waldenström macroglobulinemia with symptomatic hyperviscosity and anemia.
Plan: Plasma exchange as soon as arranged, then bendamustine plus rituximab every 28 days for six cycles. Hold off on any rituximab until IgM is lowered. Will keep you updated.
Hematology-oncology physician

documents.title: Hematology-oncology treatment update
documents.author: hematology-oncology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE CANCER CENTER — Treatment update
Plasma exchange completed 06/08 and 06/09/2020 through a temporary catheter, tolerated well. Headaches and blurred vision much improved by the second session. Cycle 1 bendamustine-rituximab given 06/22-06/23/2020. Antiemetic and infusion precautions per our protocol. Next cycle 07/20. Please continue his usual medications; no metformin change needed at current kidney function.
Hematology-oncology nurse practitioner

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Masked visit with wife. Three cycles of bendamustine-rituximab done; tired for a few days after each. Headaches and vision much better since the plasma exchange. Tingling in the feet persists. No infections.
Exam: vitals as charted. Mild pallor. Lungs clear, no edema. Stocking-glove sensory loss unchanged.
A/P:
1. WM on treatment: cancer center following CBCs.
2. Diabetes: A1c and BMP today.
3. Neuropathy symptoms: likely from the paraprotein and/or diabetes; foot care reviewed.
4. Cataract surgery set for October.
Flu shot this fall: okay per oncology timing; will coordinate.
